meta.title: Who really said "Grief is the price we pay for love"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Elizabeth II really said it: her 9/11 message, read at St Thomas Church, New York, 20 September 2001. The wording condenses psychiatrist Colin Murray Parkes.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Grief is the price we pay for love'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it is Elizabeth II's, from her 9/11 message read in New York on 20 September 2001. But the phrasing came from bereavement psychiatrist Colin Murray Parkes.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1926–2022 · Queen of the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth realms
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It is the closing sentence of the Queen’s message of condolence to the service of remembrance for British victims of the September 11 attacks, read aloud by the British ambassador Sir Christopher Meyer at St Thomas Church on Fifth Avenue, New York, on 20 September 2001, and printed in full the next morning. The thought and most of the phrasing, though, come from the bereavement psychiatrist Colin Murray Parkes.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Message from The Queen to the service of remembrance for British victims of 9/11
Sir Christopher Meyer, British ambassador to Washington
St Thomas Church, Fifth Avenue, New York · 20 September 2001
The Guardian and The Daily Telegraph, 21 September 2001

source.excerpt: These are dark and harrowing times for families and friends of those who are missing or who suffered in the attack — many of you here today. My thoughts and my prayers are with you all now and in the difficult days ahead. But nothing that can be said can begin to take away the anguish and the pain of these moments. Grief is the price we pay for love.
trail: The Guardian printed the message in full ↗, and it ends exactly on the quoted sentence — no paraphrase, no later polishing.

The Daily Telegraph of 21 September 2001 reported that the message “drew tears yesterday at a service of remembrance in New York” ↗, placing the service on 20 September 2001 — the date Wikipedia’s article on the church also gives ↗.

The parish itself treats the sentence as hers: at the first-anniversary service its rector said they “asked and were graciously given permission by Her Majesty” to carve the final sentence of her message into the memorial stone — Saint Thomas Church, 10 September 2002 ↗.
For the origin of the phrasing, WIST records Parkes’s longer 1972 sentence ↗ and his 2024 obituary carries a first-hand account of how it reached the Palace ↗.
source.excerptNote: The Guardian printed the message in full on 21 September 2001 under the standfirst “This is the text of the Queen’s message, read by the British ambassador to Washington, Sir Christopher Meyer, at the prayer service in St Thomas church, New York.” The famous line is its last sentence.

The underlying 1972 sentence in Parkes’s Bereavement: Studies of Grief in Adult Life is separately in copyright. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing either text at length is not.

author.name: Elizabeth II
author.heading: Who actually sent the message
author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Queen of the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth realms
author.bio: Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 until her death in 2022, and her public words were famously sparing — which is part of why the few sentences that landed, landed hard. The 9/11 message was written from Balmoral and sent to a church full of British families in Manhattan who had no bodies to bury. She never delivered it herself; the ambassador read it, and the congregation wept.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right for once — but almost everything around it gets garbled, starting with who wrote the words and where the Queen was when they were read.

items.who: Elizabeth II, as the coiner of the phrase
items.why: The thought and most of the wording are Colin Murray Parkes’s. In Bereavement: Studies of Grief in Adult Life (1972) he wrote: “The pain of grief is just as much a part of life as the joy of love; it is, perhaps, the price we pay for love, the cost of commitment” — quoted in full here ↗. The seven-word compression is what the Queen’s message carried.

items.who: Elizabeth II, speaking in person at a 9/11 service
items.why: She never said it aloud. The Telegraph reported that “she wrote from Balmoral” ↗ and that the British ambassador Sir Christopher Meyer read the message to the congregation.

Wikiquote’s entry dates the message 22 September 2001 ↗, but the two reports it cites are both from 21 September 2001 and describe a service held the previous day — and Wikipedia’s article on Saint Thomas Church puts the service on 20 September 2001 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Elizabeth II’s message really does end with this sentence, read at St Thomas Church on 20 September 2001 — but Cruse’s then chief executive recalls the Palace ringing the charity for advice on what the Queen might say, and Colin Murray Parkes being the man they turned to ↗.

context.heading: Why this sentence travelled
lead: The Queen was at Balmoral. The families were in Manhattan, a week after the towers came down, at a service for British dead who in most cases had no remains to bury. Her message ran only a few paragraphs, and it did not attempt consolation until the last two lines — where it stopped attempting it: “But nothing that can be said can begin to take away the anguish and the pain of these moments. Grief is the price we pay for love.”

The congregation of nearly 700 included Tony and Cherie Blair, Bill and Hillary Clinton, Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, Governor George Pataki and UN Secretary General Kofi Annan, and The Daily Telegraph reported that the message drew tears ↗. The sentence outlived the occasion almost immediately.
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the sentence afterwards
detailsBody: A year later, at the first-anniversary service for British nationals, the rector of Saint Thomas Church explained that the parish had “asked and were graciously given permission by Her Majesty” to cut the final sentence of her message into the stone beside a crucifixion memorial — his remarks are on the church’s site ↗.

After the Queen’s death in 2022, Cruse’s former chief executive Debbie Kerslake noted that the line now surfaces among her most famous quotations, and that Prince William quoted his grandmother using these words ↗ — while pointing out that the words were originally Colin Murray Parkes’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Guardian printed the full text of the Queen's message, introduced as read by British ambassador Sir Christopher Meyer at the prayer service in St Thomas church, New York, and the text ends: 'But nothing that can be said can begin to take away the anguish and the pain of these moments. Grief is the price we pay for love.'

The Daily Telegraph, 21 September 2001, reports that the Queen's message read by Sir Christopher Meyer 'drew tears yesterday at a service of remembrance in New York', that 'she wrote from Balmoral', that the congregation of almost 700 at St Thomas's Episcopal Church on Fifth Avenue included Tony and Cherie Blair, Bill and Hillary Clinton, Rudolph Giuliani, George Pataki and Kofi Annan, and it prints the closing line.

Wikipedia's article on Saint Thomas Church (Manhattan) states the September 2001 service took place on September 20, 2001 and was addressed by Prime Minister Tony Blair and broadcast live throughout the United Kingdom.

Saint Thomas Church's rector said the parish 'asked and were graciously given permission by Her Majesty' to use the final sentence of her message to the previous year's service for the crucifixion memorial, quoting 'Grief is the price we pay for love.'

Debbie Kerslake, then CEO of Cruse, recalls that after 9/11 Buckingham Palace phoned Cruse seeking advice on what the Queen might say in her message of condolence, that Cruse turned to Colin Murray Parkes, and that 'it is Colin's words - "Grief is the Price we Pay for Love" which the Queen used'; she adds that Prince William quoted his grandmother using these words after her death.

Colin Murray Parkes (6 March 1928 - 13 January 2024), British psychiatrist, wrote in Bereavement: Studies of Grief in Adult Life (1972): 'The pain of grief is just as much a part of life as the joy of love; it is, perhaps, the price we pay for love, the cost of commitment', and Queen Elizabeth II's post-9/11 message used the condensed form.

WIST records the Parkes quotation 'The pain of grief is just as much a part of life as the joy of love; it is, perhaps, the price we pay for love, the cost of commitment.' sourced to Bereavement: Studies of Grief in Adult Life (1972), noting it is sometimes shortened to 'Grief is the price we pay for love.'

Wikiquote lists among Elizabeth II's quotes: 'But nothing that can be said can begin to take away the anguish and the pain of these moments. Grief is the price we pay for love.' sourced to a message read by Sir Christopher Meyer at St Thomas's Episcopal Church on Fifth Avenue, New York, dated there as 22 September 2001, citing the 21 September 2001 Telegraph and Guardian reports.
